utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Good morning, Dr. Nakas. If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. I was told that the last document we used yesterday was not dealt with, so -- 1D1206, which was a document in the BiH Presidency. So I take it there's no opposition from the Defence, and we'll admit it as one of the Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having dealt with it, now Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: My name is Bakir Nakas, son of Mustafa and Azra Catic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And you're a doctor of medicine, by profession?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am a doctor by profession, specialising in infectious diseases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I'll proceed with the Rule 92 requirements.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, as we discussed, part of your evidence will be submitted in writing, so I need to first address some preliminary formalities associated with that submission. You provided signed statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 10th of November, 1995, the 10th and 12th of November, 1995, the 26th of February, 1996, and the 9th and 10th of October, 2001. You testified before the ICTY in the trials of Stanislav Galic on the 10th of December, 2001, and the 9th of January, 2002; in the Dragomir Milosevic case on the 25th and 29th of January, 2007; and in the Momcilo Perisic case on the 25th and 26th of March, 2009. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, it's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Subsequent to that, a statement was prepared which amalgamated evidence from your previous testimony, statements and interviews, and referenced a number of documents, which you signed on the 8th of September, 2010; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the statement on the 8th of September this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You had an opportunity to review that amalgamated witness statement and the exhibits referred to therein?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, by people from the OTP, I was shown the entire documentation, and I had the opportunity to look at the documents, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 90190, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not 91, the last two digits?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can you take it off the screen, please. Your Honour, that will require a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, 90191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, is that your statement, the amalgamated witness statement that you signed the other day?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I believe there's one amendment you wish to make. At paragraph 23, and this is on page 6 of the statement, you wish to replace the word "missiles" with the word "projectiles" so that the sentence -- the first sentence now reads: "Between 1992 and 1995, the hospital was hit with over 200 projectiles and it was subjected to direct shooting"?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Probably in the process of translation, a different term was used for the word "projectile." So I agree that instead of "missile," it should say "projectile."

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: There is also a clarification in relation to paragraph 59 and 62, and that's on page 11. There, you have a table which sets out the civilian and military patients at the State Hospital. And if we can go to the next page, in the last sentence of paragraph 61, it states that: "... the figures for the military in the above table include their civilian dependents." You wish to clarify that the military figure in the table in paragraph 59 includes: 1, JNA pensioner who remained living in Sarajevo and their dependants; 2, the members of the regular army, but not their dependants; and, 3, members of the police, but not their dependants; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, because in previous statements that I gave, some interpretations about the insurance system in the pre-war period were added to the context of the entire statement, so that it appeared that this conclusion that the total number of military beneficiaries of insurance included the members of their families. But, actually, it only includes former JNA members, retired officers, and members of their families who remained living in Sarajevo. Families of active members of the B and H Army are not included in these numbers that refer to military members. They are part of the figure that is given for civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. With that amendment and clarification, can you confirm that the statement is accurate, and that if you were asked the same questions on the same topics today, your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, I tender 65 ter 90191 for admission into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because of what part does it have to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, because of certain medical records that are on subsequent pages, from page 17 onwards. The Prosecution has up-loaded a version -- a redacted version of the witness's statement as well, so I was going to ask that that be given the next exhibit in line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done. This unredacted, amalgamated statement will be admitted as ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P1524, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the Exhibit P1525 will be a public version of that statement?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, taking out documents that are admitted under seal in another case or will be admitted under seal in this case, pursuant to Your Honour's earlier ruling at transcript 5360, pertaining to certain medical records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: With Your Honour's leave, I'll now read a brief summary of the witness's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, I take it there's no opposition from the Defence. Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- evidence. The witness is a doctor of medicine who worked as the general manager of the State Hospital in Sarajevo throughout the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina (1992 to 1995). Dr. Nakas discusses the shelling and sniping directed at the hospital throughout the war and describes its effects upon patients and staff and the overall functioning of the hospital. The witness further gives evidence in relation to the civilian casualties of the shelling and sniping campaign in Sarajevo and its effects on the civilian population. The witness authenticates selected hospital and medical records relating to scheduled sniping incidents F4, F6, F7, F9 through F12, F14 through F17, and scheduled shelling incidents G1, G4, G6, G8 through G13 and G19. Prior to the conflict, the witness worked as a doctor at Sarajevo Military Hospital as a member of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, reaching the rank of lieutenant-colonel in 1988. On the 8th of April, 1992, he requested termination from the JNA and left the hospital. Upon his return on the 10th of May, 1992, he was appointed to be general manager of the Sarajevo State Hospital, as the former military hospital was renamed. In this capacity, he was responsible for organising the entire hospital, which included establishing medical protocols and documentation for the hospital. In addition to this position as the general manager of the Sarajevo State Hospital, the witness was an adviser to the Ministry of Health of Bosnia-Herzegovina, responsible for communications regarding humanitarian aid with respect to medicines, as well as a member of the Crisis Staff, an organisation comprised of managers of all health institutions in Sarajevo. By virtue of his various positions, the witness is familiar with and can authenticate all the various forms of documentation used by all the medical and health facilities in Sarajevo. Moreover, the witness can provide statistical evaluations of patient profiles and injuries due to his position in the hospital and Ministry of Health. The witness authenticated medical documentation through his testimony in the Galic, Dragomir Milosevic and Perisic trials. In addition, the witness authenticated medical documentation in his various witness statements. Finally, the witness has viewed medical documentation and authenticated the documents. The witness described the shelling upon Sarajevo State Hospital which considerably damaged the building and severely impacted the proper functioning of the hospital, despite the placement of a Red Cross flag on the building. From personal observations of the shelling, the types of shell fragments found at the hospital, and the placement of the damage primarily upon the south side of the hospital, the witness determined that the source of fire was the area under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In addition to shelling upon the hospital, the hospital's staff and patients were victims of sniper fire, which injured a number of people. Again, from the placement of the sniper fire damage, the witness determined the source of the fire to be the area under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. The shelling and sniping campaign in Sarajevo impacted the hospital's access to utilities and medicine, resulting in the provision of medical services under the most dire circumstances. When large numbers of patients came to the hospital as a result of the shelling, the Markale Market shelling in 1995, for example, the witness was able to observe that most of the wounded or killed were civilians or military members who were off duty. The impact of the shelling and sniping campaign upon the population of Sarajevo, in general, and upon the patients and staff of the Sarajevo State Hospital, in particular, resulted in mental as well as physical problems. Heightened emotions, fear, and depression were common, particularly since the population faced the risk of death on a daily basis. All people in Sarajevo of all ethnicities were equally exposed to the stress of the war. That concludes the brief summary of the witness's evidence. Your Honour, in our filing on last Friday, we had indicated that we had increased the witness's time from 15 minutes to half an hour. I wish to deal with a couple of areas, asking the witness a few questions, which should take no longer than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, in paragraph 5 of your amalgamated witness statement, you stated you were appointed as the general manager of the hospital. And in paragraph 79 of the statement, you state that as administrator, you were and continue to be authorised to authenticate copies of medical documents. In paragraph 93(a) of your statement --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- which is on page 26, but we won't bring that up, it was a list of medical records that you authenticated in your witness statements of the 10th of November, 1995, and the 9th and 10th of October, 2001. These were documents that you reviewed last week, and previously authenticated in the two statements I referred to, by either providing original medical records or certified copies of such records; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do these same records that are listed appear to be hospital or medical records ordinarily produced in the regular course of business?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the result of the services provided daily by all the hospitals, by the Clinical Centre, the Dobrinja Hospital, the Emergency Service. So it's definitely a type of communication and affirmation or confirmation of certain information essential for patients and also for the purposes of the treatment.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the topic of statistics. In paragraph 91 of the statement, you discuss there a document. Perhaps before that: In your position as the general manager of the State Hospital, did you receive reports in relation to a number of patients -- the number of patients treated in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That was standard procedure for purposes of planning of a certain activity and in order to report to the authorised institutions. Data was grouped every day that was arriving from the Emergency Centre and other hospital services, which comprised collective data about the daily activities of our institution, providing care to the wounded, the injured, or cases of medical treatment for those who were suffering from classic diseases.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If I could ask for Exhibit P01242, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: This is the document that's the exhibit referred to in paragraph 91 of your statement. Looking at page 1 of the B/C/S and page 1 and 2 of the English, we can see that this is a report of the Emergency Centre of the Surgical Department and, over on page 2 in the English, of the Gynaecological Department for the month of December 1994. Who generated this report, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The reports are a summary of monthly activities of the Surgical/Emergency Centre of the Sarajevo State Hospital, as well as the report of the Gynaecology Department of the same hospital. They were drafted by medical technicians in both cases who were in charge of generating this data. In the specific case, it was the medical technician from the Emergency Centre responsible for those tasks, and from the Gynaecology Department it was the chief nurse of that department. The reports are, in essence, a collection of data of the most important activities, and they were previously designed for these purposes of monitoring the number of newly wounded, admitted, number of surgeries, and some other data.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: How was this data generated; from what?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The data comes from the Official Protocols, the book registering all the patients who were admitted and treated in the Emergency Centre; in the second case, those who were treated at the Gynaecology Department. This is data recorded in the period of one month. At the end of the month, the data was compiled and presented to me so that I would be able to use it for various purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 2 in the B/C/S and pages 3 to 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, we can see here that it's a report on the number and type of surgeries for December 1994. Who generated this report?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The report comes from the Central Surgery Section, which was part of the Surgery Ward/Department of the hospital. And the data collects data on the number of surgeries, the types of surgeries, the chief surgeon, the assistant, the anesthesiologist, the number of surgeries according to the type of patients to the type of wounded, and the workload by surgery operating room. The task for compiling these reports was given to the medical technician who was in charge of the operation of the Central Surgical Block. The data was generated on the basis of the monthly number of interventions in the Central Surgery Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And, again, from where were these figures taken from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: These figures were taken from the protocols of interventions in the Central Surgical Block of the Surgery Department. They have nothing to do with the protocol of the Emergency Centre and the figures that are cited there, other than the fact that those patients who were processed through the Emergency Centre could later end up in the Surgical Section.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We see here, at number 10, the number of surgeries by the type of wounding. Did these reports also include a report on amputations performed?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Specifically in this report, that data is not given. However, in later reports that were part of these documents, the number of amputations is given, performed within a certain time-period, and specifically that number was entered there because my superiors and the international community sought information about the number of amputees so that they could plan for certain types of aid, for artificial limbs and other kinds of prosthetics. This information is not in each report, only in some of the reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who was Dr. Abdulah Nakas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Dr. Abdulah Nakas was my brother. He passed away in 2005, in November. Throughout the war, he was the chief surgeon in my hospital, and he was in charge of the Surgical Department. After his death, in 2006, at the request of citizens from Sarajevo and the surrounding area, the Assembly of the Sarajevo Canton renamed the hospital, naming it after Abdulah Nakas, honouring everything he did in the previous period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 in the B/C/S and pages 5 to 6 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, here we see: "Citizens of Sarajevo who were wounded by sniper shot and taken care in the Emergency Centre," for the period August to December 1994 and January to October 1995. Who generated this report?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The report that is before you was compiled by myself, personally, in 2007, at the request of the Tribunal. An interest was expressed in view of the information concerning the total number of citizens from Sarajevo who were wounded by sniper fire in 1994 and in 1995; from August to December 1994 and from January to October 1995, that is. This was prepared for the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And when you say "at the request of the Tribunal," do you -- are you referring to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And how was this report generated? Where were the figures taken from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: These figures were taken from the protocol of the Emergency Centre; namely, the books from August to December 1994 and from January to October 1995. I went through them personally, I looked at the figures myself, and I compiled the report that is before you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the three separate documents that we have just looked at, if I understood you correctly a moment ago, are not interrelated, but there can be some overlap, is that right, because the protocol is the source of the information?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Your Honours. The previous two documents were produced during the course of our work every month, and they had to do with what had been tasked earlier on. However, this is a report that was specially compiled related to the number of cases that were treated in the mentioned periods. Practically all of these documents use one-and-the-same source. However, they present data on the basis of what this report looks like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this exhibit has 35 pages in B/C/S and 70 pages in English. You reviewed the entirety of this exhibit. Is it right that all the reports contained in this exhibit are reports which were produced in the ordinary course of business, except, of course, for this document which we see on the screen, which you prepared for the Dragomir Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It is exactly as you had stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P01238, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, what is this document which is shown on the screen?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the left-hand side in the version in our language, we see a photocopy of one page of the protocol that was used during the course of the work of the State Hospital of Sarajevo. There are certain rubrics here that have to be filled out. There is a certain method of coding, and there are certain codes that are listed here. They were in use while it was a military hospital; that is to say, while members of the JNA were being treated there and when reports were being sent to superiors in Belgrade. In the period from 1992 until 1995, we continued using identical protocols. However, the way records were kept was changed. We did not use those codes anymore, but we actually filled this out in the way in which it had been recorded; namely, the date of the examination, the number of protocol, the number of the record involved, the name and surname of the patient, the year of birth, the category involved, and we would put the diagnosis. We would also provide comments as to the kind of medical intervention that was carried out, and also there is the decision of the physician who examined the doctor [as interpreted], whether a patient was being admitted into hospital or being examined and then sent back home, and would continue to be treated as an outpatient. This is what we call a protocol in our day-to-day life.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. That can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, I now wish to turn to focus on the shelling and sniping of the State Hospital. In paragraph 4 of your statement, you said that you returned to the hospital on the 10th of May. In paragraph 34 of your statement, you stated that the worst period of targeting on the hospital was from the 13th to the 16th of May, 1992, when the hospital was hit by about 40 shells of various kinds, mainly tank and artillery shells. And in paragraph 23, you state that between 1992 and 1995, the hospital was hit with over 200 projectiles and it was subject to direct shooting. Finally, in paragraphs 23 to 24, and paragraph 31, you state that the source of the shelling and sniper fire emanated from the area of Trebevic, Osmice, Vrace and Grbavica, which was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska. What's the basis of your conclusion that the shelling was the responsibility of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all of those who lived in the encircled Sarajevo during this period of time knew quite clearly which part of our city was held by which forces and from which positions shelling or sniping against the citizens of Sarajevo was taking place. It's not only that we could confirm this and know this; this was confirmed by the international community as well. It was confirmed by the observers. It was proven through previous statements made by all persons who spent a certain period of time during the aggression in Sarajevo. As a Sarajevo-born person, I know certain parts of town. I know roughly what the ethnic affiliation of the population was. I also know about the abrupt changes that took place after the 2nd of March, after the barricades were put up in Sarajevo. Some people were taken and others voluntarily went to the areas that were under the control of the authorities of the Sarajevo government. The neighbourhood around my hospital was evidently under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska; at first also of part of the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA. They held large areas. They had their manpower and artillery in different barracks. I'm primarily referring to Lukavica and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You said that the damage to the hospital was primarily on the south side in -- you deal with this issue in paragraphs 19 to 33?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Correct. The southern side was closest to the line of separation. It had been damaged the most, too. On the southern side, if I may correct what you said at the outset, when you said that the flag was on the roof of the hospital, the flag was on the southern side, that is to say, from the roof towards the southern side, and then it was lowered down to a particular floor. It was an attempt made by the management to provide additional information to those who were supposed to know that this is a medical facility, a medical facility only, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 10452.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Doctor, what is shown in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, you can see in this photograph the southern side of the State Hospital of Sarajevo. This photograph was taken from the middle of Dolina Street; that is, on the approaches to the hospital. On the top, you see a flag of the Red Cross, you see the different floors of the building, and you see where there are windows and where there are not windows. And in most places, there aren't any windows. On the southern side, most of the foreigners who came to this hospital called it the Swiss Cheese Hospital, and that is how they readily recognised it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's referred to in paragraph 22 of -- that photograph, in paragraph 22 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1526, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, who was in control of the territory to the south of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The southern side of the hospital was facing part of the Miljacka and the slopes of Trebevic and Vraca. The separation line was practically the Miljacka River, Vrbanja Most, Grbavica, so it's that area and those slopes that directly faced the hospital. That area was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: What, if anything, were you able to observe from the hospital when the shelling was occurring?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Well, definitely, when the hospital was being shelled, I had the opportunity of seeing where this was happening. I had the opportunity of freely assessing this on the basis of the openings that were made and the damage caused by the projectile. I could see where the projectile had come from. If we are talking about other possibilities, if you went to the top floors, sometimes you could even see the firing position that a projectile would be fired from because you could see the trail of smoke.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And this was in relation to all of the areas that we have just mentioned previously?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It pertains to these areas and others that are mentioned in my statement, when I spoke about the beginning of the shelling of the city of Sarajevo, not only the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In paragraph 48 of your statement, you state that it appeared to you that the Serbs were intent on destroying vital parts of the hospital, and you base this on the fact that, in your view, they were targeting specific floors of the hospital. Is there any other reason why you are of the view that the Serbs were intent on destroying the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Some messages that we received when the previous staff was leaving the hospital on the 9th and 10th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not personally hear this. It was my staff who heard this. As they were leaving, they were promising to destroy the hospital once they left, once they moved all of their forces out and once they no longer used the premises. This is what a medical technician said from a particular department. Another factor involved in hitting the vital parts of the hospital is based on what I heard from Professor Enver Hadzimustafic, who is a professor at the School of Architecture of the University of Sarajevo. From the beginning of the shelling, he made certain estimates, and he told me that the eighth floor is the weakest point in the hospital building, and there are a few pillars there, and one was hit during the initial shelling in May 1992. This confirmed that feeling for me, that is to say, this wish to destroy the hospital. That was evident by virtue of the fact that they were hitting that part of the hospital, not other parts, or, rather, other parts were hit less. In addition to that, I can say that also on several occasions what was targeted were the operating theaters, a vital part of the hospital. Also, parts of the hospital that are of vital importance for the maintenance of the hospital and parts of the hospital that were essential for logistics purposes; namely, the preparation of food, and clothing, and sterilisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything at any Crisis Staff -- Crisis Centre meetings about the intention to destroy the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. As a member of the Crisis Staff, at first I had an opportunity of meeting the heads of key medical institutions of Sarajevo. That was on a daily basis at first and, later on, a weekly basis. They were the heads of the health centres and the emergency centres. At one of these meetings in the beginning of 1992, or, rather, between May and June, we had some information to the effect that Dragan Kalinic, our hitherto colleague, at that point minister of health of Republika Srpska, had instructions for those who were shelling Sarajevo; namely, that they should focus their fire at the Clinical Centre, because if the capacities of that hospital were to be diminished, the citizenry would feel less safe and medical professionals would not have an opportunity of doing their job.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That completes my examination-in-chief, Your Honour. I seek to tender the associated exhibits, and that is all the exhibits listed in Appendix A and Confidential Appendix B which have not already been admitted. Did Your Honour have the Rule 92 notification in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dated when?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The 8th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I have it before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So on page -- Appendix A in the list of associated exhibits, on the second page of those associated exhibits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are many items that have already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But of the first four -- the first three, I can read the 65 ter numbers if you wish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: So the associated exhibits start with a number of the witness statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... which we don't seek to tender through him. So the first one is 09519, 10378, 10162 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Give me a minute. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Then the one that follows that has just been admitted. That's the photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And so the next one is 10163.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And that is all on that page, because the remaining two exhibits -- the remaining two have been exhibited already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: On the following page, none of these exhibits, because the bottom one, 10418, is, in fact, P00459.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And on the following page, the last exhibit, 09991, 65 ter number. And then in Confidential Appendix B, all of the documents on page 1 and page 2. And then the second-to-last one is a duplication because it's listed on page 1 of Confidential Appendix B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We are on the last page of the Confidential Annex?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second item you --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Second-to-last item.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have difficulty following all --

utterances.text: Again, if it assists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will check everything later on, and then with consultation with the Court Deputy, I will let the parties know the exhibit numbers assigned to those exhibits which have not been already tendered --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- if it is agreeable to the parties, and then we'll put those confidential documents under seal. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We don't object to the associated exhibits. And if there are spreadsheets that include both protected witnesses and non-protected witnesses, we would ask that they be submitted with the KDZ number substituted for the name of those who were protected witnesses and submitted not under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that was my understanding of Your Honour's earlier ruling which I referred to earlier today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be done outside the courtroom. Our Legal Officers will consult -- the Court Deputy should consult the Legal Officers. Those numbers will be informed in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you start, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Nakas.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would first of all like to thank you for meeting with the Defence. This will help us to be specific about a large number of things and to finish more quickly. And I regret not knowing you before, because we could have fought together for the preservation of Yugoslavia. That position of yours on the preservation of Yugoslavia was a large, pleasant surprise for me. Dr. Nakas, you have a statement here of 96 paragraphs, and you confirmed that you stand by that statement. Is the information in these paragraphs something from your direct experience and should be considered in the record as your contribution to the evidence?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, all the information in all of the 96 paragraphs is my knowledge about the events in the period from 1992 to 1995 in Sarajevo. As for whether I am the author, or just a participant, or just the person with knowledge of these events is not that relevant. What is relevant is that I stand by the information as a participant, to a degree, as somebody who received some information, and as somebody who was aware of some information that everyone else was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Why I'm asking this is because my learned colleague, Ms. Sutherland, spent one hour. I also have one hour. I have 96 paragraphs of yours to go through, so it would help me if you were able to indicate some of those paragraphs and say that this is something that you had heard, so that I would not have to go through all of those paragraphs and deal with their reliability. Are there any paragraphs that you would not stand by in this statement?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the paragraphs where the knowledge is second-hand knowledge are very few. They are practically nonexistent. The paragraphs contain my knowledge, my conviction that those things did take place, which was confirmed by people with whom I spent my work hours in occupied Sarajevo, and for that reason none of the paragraphs is of such a nature that I could point to it and say I no longer stand by this paragraph because what is there does no longer stand. I was a participant or I have strong conviction that those who conveyed this information to you -- to me were properly informed. So there is no hearsay in any of the paragraphs, and definitely there is nothing there that is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nakas. Then you will understand that I will have to go through each one of those paragraphs in order not to let them stand as possible grounds for a future conviction. Can we now look at the map of the town. This is Map 13 from the map compilation. This is ERN 0546-6581. We were practicing this a little bit, marking the map and all the locations, so I hope that this would be somewhat easier for you now. I would be very grateful to Ms. Sutherland if she could help us. This is 0546-6581, Map 13 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a part of a broken-down map, yes. I hope Mr. Reid could help us.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: 65 ter 13519, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. Thank you. Can we please zoom it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, Dr. Nakas, do you agree that this is the map of town, the old town and the center, and that we can see the town from the railway station to Bascarsija to Bembasa?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the part of town, including the locations referred to from old town -- including the old town and the center.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now zoom in on the left third, between Kovaci and Kovacici, precisely where the cursor is. Could we zoom in on that part of the map, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, can I ask you to mark the complex of the Military Hospital and to briefly tell us what the buildings are? You can mark and indicate -- tell us what each building is.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The complex of the State Hospital of Sarajevo is on the map, marked with this red line [marks]. There is a group of buildings that are interconnected. This is the oldest part of the hospital, where the administration and the poly clinic are. That's this part here [marks]. And then the part where the diagnostics activity takes place, it's connected to this other building. And then the central part --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, since this is a hospital, are you able to mark these buildings with 1, 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is number 1 [marks]. This is the poly clinic building and the administration buildings. Number 2 is the central building with diagnostics and the Emergency Centre on the ground floor [marks]. Then we have number 3. That is that part of the building here [marks], and that is the central building that has 12 floors. It's a little bit difficult -- actually, there is no dominant line here. It's all along one line, so it's not quite correct on the map. This part here [marks] is where the logistics are. This is where the kitchen, the laundry are, and other areas. And then this is the ground floor annex where patients also were placed [marks]. This part here is the old military hospital and the hostel which was not used in the aggression -- during the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the layout and the location of the facilities of the Sarajevo State Hospital in the period from 1992 to 1995 [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Mr. Karadzic may be going to get the witness to repeat again what stands for number 4 and number 5 that he's just marked on the map, because the transcript is going to be unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Doctor, if you could tell us what those number 4 and number 5 mean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the numbers 4 and 5 -- first 4. "4" indicates the number of the hospital where the logistics are situated; the kitchen, the laundry, and all those other services essential for the functioning of the hospital, in terms of logistics. The number of the building -- the part of the building marked with the "5" is the building where patients are placed. This is a four-floor hospital facility, and all of these buildings are interconnected. If you enter one side, you can leave through the other end, and they are interconnected with a series of underground passages and certain hallways. They constitute the connection between the various buildings. This is a very modern facility built by the Yugoslav People's Army. It designed it, and it was built for its own needs. And in the former Yugoslavia, this was the third-ranking hospital after Belgrade and Zagreb Hospitals. Unfortunately, in the aggression large parts of this beautiful hospital could not be used, and our lives, actually, during the first years went on mostly in the basement cellars and protected areas, where our patients were located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us, Dr. Nakas, so that we can avoid confusion? If we're talking about the Military Hospital, and then the State Hospital, and then the City Hospital, and then the French Hospital and the Dr. Abdulah Nakas Hospital, are we referring to one-and-the-same hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct, this is one-and-the-same hospital which up until 1992 was called the Military Hospital; then from May 25th, 1992, was referred to as the State Hospital of Sarajevo. For a brief period of time the people referred to it as the French Hospital because there were rumours that France would protect the hospital in some way. This never took place and it was never officially named the French Hospital. After that, in 2000 it became the General Hospital of Sarajevo. And then after the death of my brother in 2005, it has been called Dr. Abdulah Nakas General Hospital of Sarajevo. So when we're talking about all of these names, we're talking about the same hospital, and the people most often actually referred to it as the former Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now let's look at number 5. Number 5 is an old building which you said was a hostel, and the hospital did not use that building during the war. What was in that building or who was in that building during the war?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: That is not number 5. This is the separate building here which I'm marking with the number 6 [marks]. That building was not used during the first half, practically until autumn 1992, when it was requisitioned by the 1st Corps as a building. And then that building and another building that is not shown here were used as a rehabilitation centre for the treatment and surgery of members of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that with a number 7, this place where the soldiers went for treatment and rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So 6 and 7 were requisitioned by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina towards the end of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can you please mark the old Military Hospital between the Kranjcevica and Marsala Tita Street? Could you mark that location and also put a number there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was in that building before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for your information, this is where the first Turkish Military Hospital was built in 1866, so we are their successors. Before the events in question in 1992, it was abandoned. The Military Hospital personnel moved to the new building, and this old building was handed over to the Romanija Military Enterprise which supplied the armed forces members with food. We had some workshops in a part of this building, also some warehouses for technical parts for surgery, tables and some equipment that we used, so we used this until 1992. Until 1992, this was more in the property of the Romanija Military Company, and our ownership of it was not a factor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark the mosque?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The mosque is not marked here, but we do see the Magribija Street, and we have this building which is immediately above the Military Hospital. I know that area, I live and work there, so I know that on the opposite side of this wall there was the Magribija Mosque. It was there then, and it's still there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark this with the number 9?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's not Marsala Tita. Actually, could you indicate with an arrow that it's more towards the letter G?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, how many mosques does Sarajevo have, roughly?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Quite a few, quite a few, but never enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many of them were hit?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: A larger number were hit. Specifically, in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo, some were destroyed. Those that were in the center were also destroyed. Practically, not a single one was razed to the ground, but there were some physical damages involved; perhaps the minaret was destroyed or the roof, but none of them were totally destroyed, physically, because none of them ever fell into the hands of those into whose hands they were not supposed to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I'm going to put something to you now; that only Magribija and the mosque at Kobilja Glava had been hit, the others remained intact. Do you know that the Magribija Mosque was an arms depot of the Green Berets and that fire was opened at the Military Hospital from the minaret of that mosque?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I do not consider that assertion to be correct at all, absolutely not. That is what you are saying. I know that Magribija was used for prayer whenever possible. As for what you're saying now, this is very, very new information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to show documents about that. Could you link these three levels of Avdo Jabucica Street to the north?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: On the map, you can see that there is practically two parts of this street that are named Avdo Jabucica, this part and that part [marks]. There's a bit of a climb involved, so it is an S-shaped street. It's in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you use a vertical line to connect all of them there? I see three levels of Avdo Jabucica Street, and I remember the layout of the street. When I went looking for some friends of mine, I had trouble finding them.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is like a serpentine; you're right. Now, is that Crni Vrh, this Elevation 614?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: According to the map, you can see that the name is Crni Vrh and the elevation is 614, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Do you know that below Crni Vrh, below the street of Omera Stupca, on that clearing there there was a Howitzer?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I hear of it, from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're going to believe a map of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I hope. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you show that?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to say, could the accused please put a time-frame with his questions? Just for the record, can we note that the witness marked number 8 as the old Military Hospital, because that is not in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it's time to have a break. We can keep this for the moment, or shall we ask the witness to put the date and your signature on the map, with the assistance of our usher, please? Could you write down the date, which is 14th of September.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your signature, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, but we'll go back to this because we need to have some other things marked on this map as well. So perhaps we can deal with that later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll continue with this map. We'll have a break for 20 minutes and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Just a few more notes on this map, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark the Unis buildings, one circle around Momo and the other one around Uzeir? One is a Serb name, the other is a Muslim name, and these are the names that people popularly refer to as a joke.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It's in this part [marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we in trouble? We saved that already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If that's the way it is, can we see the total of the map, because we need to mark a few other locations, and then we're done with the map. The left -- or, rather, the two-thirds of the map on the left, could we have that? Has this been assigned a number, anyway?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we keep this, and then -- ah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Momo and Uzeir, can you mark those two Unis buildings? You need a pen, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This seems to be a somewhat different one. Just in case, we'll give the exhibit number which has been already marked, just in case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D615.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have the two-thirds of the map that are on the left, or can we see the entire map once again so that we don't disrupt anything in any way. Perhaps we can have it as a new exhibit. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can you mark the Unis buildings here? Actually, we don't see Debelo Brdo and the Kosevo Tunnel. We need a bit more, so we actually have to have a different scale. Can we see the lower and the upper margins, if possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we bring up the 65 ter 13519.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's what I meant. It can remain as it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you put a circle around the Military Hospital, and then Ciglane, and then the Kosevo Tunnel?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, now the map is a bit different, in terms of its dimensions, so it's easy for me to put a circle around the Sarajevo State Hospital [marks]. Then Ciglane, that's a bit more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can't you see it? It's written up there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I could only imagine that this is Ciglane, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But it's written there and you can see it, can't you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Not on my map. I can't read any of the names, except for those that are in big letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the north, Kovaci and then Ciglane?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It's this part here, sorry. Yes, this part [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark that as number 2? Put a circle and write number 2 there, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the Kosevo Tunnel, the Kosevo Tunnel, could you mark that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Number 1 is the State Hospital. Then now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the north, way up north.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It's possible that it's somewhere around here [marks]. Ciglane is here, and then it could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, it's towards the very top.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Ah, the top. As far as I know, this is a railroad leading to the railway station. So in that area, the only possible position of the tunnel would be somewhere around here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance. Do you remember the hill of Kosevo and then the tunnel? It's to the north, further north. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up here at the very top, it says "Cemetery" in English.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. The tunnel can be seen, it's marked, but it's at the very top, at the very edge of this image. Oh, it's all right. Can you see Debelo Brdo down there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: That's what's written here, "Debelo Brdo."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark it as number 3, because we haven't marked the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I now ask you to put a circle around the bridge on Vrbanja?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That would be number 4. Then the bridge at Skenderija and the place where, on the 2nd of May, people who left the Military Hospital going to Dom Armija got killed.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's number 5, isn't it? Now, the Unis buildings, please.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, can you mark Astra that we discussed already?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, during our interview we discussed these buildings that are in the immediate vicinity of Momo and Uzeir. These are residential buildings in Kranjcevica Street, and we discussed that whether -- I was asked whether Astra, the building of Astra was there. However, it was Alpina that was there, not Astra. The Astra building actually relates to a completely different building in New Sarajevo, in a neighbourhood that is very close to the TV station. In this high-rise, there is a store, a shoe store, Alpina, not Astra, so my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I agree. Do you know that Alpina was a facility of the Green Berets during the war?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Unis buildings -- I apologise to the interpreters, but I am so pressed for time. Do you know that the Unis buildings were a military facility, that the command of a unit was there, and that they were firing from those buildings?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I witnessed the torching of these two buildings in May and June 1992, so I watched this with my very own eyes. I watched the buildings burn. So it was not possible for anyone to be staying there, except for birds, if there were any in Sarajevo at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to say, Doctor, that not even on the ground floor or in the basement there could be no command of a military unit and that these skyscrapers were not being used to fire at buildings around them?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. Again, I did not go there myself, physically, because we had considered themselves to be abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark the Catholic Church at Marin Dvor, in relation to Trscanska Street, for instance? It's where number 8 is, if I may lead in that way.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So can you assign number 7 to Alpina and number 8 to the Catholic Church?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that right by the Catholic Church, there was the logistics base of a brigade, probably King Tvrtko?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I know that in the immediate vicinity of the Catholic Church, the Police Administration was located there, Centar, the one that was in charge of the safety and security of citizens in the area. As for the location of any military unit in that area, I really have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my second question, and you've already responded. Can you mark the Zagreb Hotel, please, in relation to what you've marked so far? Is that in the continuation of Magribija or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It's approximately here [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you mark that with number 9, please?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Hotel Zagreb was turned into a Green Beret military facility? Actually, later it was the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina later?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I know that for a while refugees were put up in that hotel. I don't know where military facilities were located. I didn't hear that that was it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you circle, next to the police building -- can you -- the building of the Police Service, because that was related to military action, do you see it? Can you circle the police building?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: If this is Veliki Park --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is Trampina and Veliki Park, so then it's higher up as you go farther. It's a large building, the only large building in black there. Is that the police building? It's fork-shaped.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Well, it's possible, but there is no indication that it could be so. If this is Veliki Park, then the building could be that one, because it's right at the top of that park [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please circle that and mark it with a number.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you also just draw the line along the Miljacka River where the line of separation was? This is towards the hospital.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: For us, the Miljacka River was the separation line, practically. So up to this bridge [marks], and from the bridge on it was behind this side and upwards in this direction [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please encircle the buildings of the Parliament and the building of the Government of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: This is the Parliament building and this is the Government building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you mark them with numbers 11 and 12, please?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was between Vrbanja, the Serbian positions, and the Military Hospital? Who was keeping this territory?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The territory between Vrbanja and the State Hospital was under the control of the army, that is to say, under the control of the regular authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you think that Serbs were not the regular authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, even though we won one-third of authorities in 1990?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I just know the regular Bosnia and Herzegovina that was recognised by international authorities and that was confirmed at the referendum in March 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us not deal with this topic. Let me ask you this: In one of your statements, you say that you were aware that Serbs planned to cut through the city. I will find which protocol it is. Let me try to locate the paragraph. How do you know that Serbs or the JNA planned to cut through the city? Who planned to cut through the city? Can you specify who it was, and what was the line that they planned?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, having certain information about the situation in the State Hospital and the Military Hospital immediately before I left it on the 8th of April, the Yugoslav People's Army did not plan to abandon these facilities. When I was the head of the Contagious Diseases Department, even though I was excluded from many activities in early 1992, though I was an equal member, the information about the possible abandoning of these facilities was nonexistent. Another fact that convinced me was that the equipment from the former Military Hospital, on the 9th and 10th of May, was not dismantled and taken away; I mean, the basic equipment. That means that they did not plan to use it elsewhere. The third fact, suggesting the intention to cut through the city in May and attack the Presidency building with tanks which appeared at the Skenderija Bridge, it was evident, even for a layman, that there was an intention to cut the city of Sarajevo in two parts along Djuro Djakovic Street, which is hereabouts [marks], so that the western part would then be under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, whereas the central part would remain fully encircled. And the third -- or, rather, the fourth fact was the fierceness of the Pofalici battle, which was intended to be used in order to occupy that part of Sarajevo at any cost and move the separation line all the way to Alipasina Street. I was a soldier partly by profession, and that allowed me to assess that that was the plan of the part of the Yugoslav People's Army which sided itself with the other side, and also the intention of the members of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, you have expanded this to include many unreliable facts, and, therefore, I have a lot of work to do. Let us try to agree about this. Were the Marsal Tito Barracks and the Military Hospital facilities that were owned by the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Not precisely the Yugoslav People's Army, but rather the Federal Secretariat of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And its organ was the Yugoslav People's Army; correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, it was one of its functional organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And was there a plan to cut the city in two, connected with the intention to take hold of their property and also to pull out the soldiers from Marsal Tito Barracks?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As a citizen of Sarajevo, I can just say that in one moment there was an agreement to evacuate the personnel from Marsal Tito Barracks, and that they were peacefully evacuated, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was in the month of June; correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, when did tanks appear in Skenderija, and where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The tanks appeared on the 2nd of May, as far as I have learned, and they had come from the direction of Grbavica, or, rather, from Lukavica, Vrace and Grbavica. That was the only possible route from which a tank could have come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I will now tell you that there were no tanks anywhere on the 2nd of May. In the place which you marked with number 5, I believe, on the 2nd of May, in two ambulances and one open Pinzgauer, the crew from the Military Hospital, which set off to evacuate the wounded from the Army Centre, and this is documented, there were no tanks anywhere on the 2nd of May, and these people died, they were practically burned, two ambulances and one Pinzgauer; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I left the former Military Hospital on the 8th of April, 1992, so the information as to who was staying at the hospital is not something I had directly and personally, but I heard it from people who were there. So on the 2nd of May, I was not physically present at the hospital, but what I do know from later conversations and from recordings and broadcasts by the Sarajevo TV, the persons we are talking about now were not personnel of the Military Hospital. No Military Hospital staff member was either wounded or killed. These were primarily members of a special unit from Nis, the Nis specialists who, immediately after I left, I think, on the 10th of April, entered the Military Hospital and took over its security, under quotation marks. They took control of all the higher floors, took certain positions, and in the office in which I had been the chief until the 8th of May, was now accommodated the chief of that unit. What I learned was that the ambulances and the Pinzgauer contained members of the special unit from Nis and not a single staff member of the Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, and we have documents about that as well. And on the 3rd of May, Doctor, were there any tanks on that date, or am I right that on the 3rd of May there was another convoy of the JNA which was leaving with the guarantees of the president of the Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, and the supervision of General MacKenzie, was moving in the opposite direction, but that then the convoy was cut through and some people were killed there?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know about this transport and the incident that happens, but I do not have any information about the specific circumstances, just as I do not know much about the death of these members of the special unit. I don't have direct information, and I use the date just as my assessment about the plans to cut through this part of the city and divide it into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, this is more of a discussion between yourself and the witness, rather than a cross-examination, and the danger of it is exactly as is being produced. The witness is being encouraged to go beyond the evidence in his statement and to make assumptions and repeat hearsay that he's heard. This is not to doubt his ability to do that. I'm not talking about credibility. I'm talking about ability to do it. But it's going to expand on the evidence enormously, which is something that you are complaining about, but you are actually creating this expansion rather than identifying parts of the witness's evidence which you can test and asking him closed, specific questions. Of course, you can ask leading questions, you're cross-examining, but asking him specific questions about those matters. The danger is that this will become an open-ended discussion and go well beyond the time allocated to you, without you having dealt with the essential material issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And we lost the marked map. But you spent more than half an hour, almost 40 minutes, with the witness, asking the witness to mark the map, which turned out to be useless because the witness was not able to confirm anything about what you stated, your statement which you put to the witness. So it's a total waste of time. Spend your time efficiently. You have spent 45 minutes, and please try to conclude your cross-examination in 20 minutes. Ask relevant questions which should be put to this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please bring back the map and admit it as an exhibit? And as for concluding, it is impossible for me to question this witness. I was allowed one hour because the OTP announced that their direct examination would last 15 minutes, but they have quadrupled that, so it is to be expected that the cross-examination time would also be quadrupled. If we work in this way and if the speed is detrimental for the Defence, then I will certain believe that this witness has not been properly cross-examined. There are 96 paragraphs, and the witness stands by all of them. He claims that this is truth which he checked by direct information. This is something I cannot accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: All I can say, that calculation should not be done in that way of pro rata. His evidence is mainly in written evidence, his amalgamated statement. The fact that the Prosecution spent more time than anticipated has a certain bearing, but that should not be calculated as you put it, pro rata. I was told that we can use the video image of that map later on to up-load and give the number, but at the moment in the e-court, we lost the marked map. Yes, Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: If it assists, it isn't necessary, even though you don't agree with everything in the witness's evidence, to go through it paragraph by paragraph. You can make the point, as you have, that you don't accept the conclusions. The Court will understand that. The evidence that you produce in due course to counteract the material contained in the statement is what will be the evidence in the case, and it will be up to the Trial Chamber to compare and contrast and put it into context with all the other evidence that is heard. But you don't have to go through every paragraph with the witness and, as it were, argue the point. The Court is well aware that you will be contesting those matters which are detrimental to your case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll give you until the end of this session, which means by 12.00. So you should be able to conclude your cross-examination by noon today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please remove the map. Can the number be assigned to the previous map, the total, so that we could save it from the video? And could we now see 1D00418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The second marked map will be exhibited as Exhibit D616. And just in case, why don't we admit the clean version of this map for reference purposes. That will be admitted as Exhibit D617. And let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see 1D00418. Thank you. I'm not sure if we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, just briefly, I will direct your attention to this document from the 1st Corps, sent to Amir Deljkic, deputy -- no, assistant commander of the 7th Mountain or Bosnian Brigade, and it says, for example: "The HVO units," if you look at the third paragraph, "The HVO unit located at Marin Dvor," according to information received from Nermin Eminovic or Aminovic [phoen], assistant commander of the district staff of the defence of Sarajevo for security, is directly connected to the OKBO Sarajevo, and it's an integral part of the 12th Mountain Brigade. This assistant also provided us with the following information: HVO units in Mejtas, in [indiscernible] Street, are connected with the Main Staff of the HVO," and so on. The HOS unit is deployed in Avdo Jabucica Street. It's a kind of military police, and it's under the command of the HOS staff. Is it the Avdo Jabucica Street which is behind the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, there is only one Avdo Jabucica Street in Sarajevo, and perhaps this part of text might be referring to this street.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please admit this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D618, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we please now see 1D02110.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While this appears on the screen, Doctor - let us not show the photograph of the hospital again - two questions. What damage of the building dates before the 10th of May and what damage was sustained after the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: We are talking about the State Hospital again, so not the Military Hospital, I mean the former Military Hospital. In the photograph, 99.9 per cent of all damage was caused after the 10th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how do you calculate that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I wasn't calculating at all. When I returned to the hospital on the 10th of May, I entered through that door, and I looked at the southern facade with my very own eyes. On it, I could see a hole where probably a Zolja had hit the building, and there was a number of small points of damage on the building which looked like damage caused by small arms. There were instances -- no instances of other damage, such as broken windows.
