utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was shooting at the Military Hospital before the 10th of May?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the 10th of May, that is to say, until the 8th of April, I was working at the hospital, and I did not personally see that anyone shot a single shot at the hospital, at least not in the parts of the building that I was moving through. And I was in the four-storey building, also in the central building, in the administration building at the 12th floor, and I did not have any information that anything like that happened. After my departure and after the entry of the Nis Special Unit, which probably began to use the facility for different purposes at that time, it is possible that in order to respond to provocation from certain parts, the forces located in the city responded in one way or another.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, two or three things. The Nis Special Unit is a unit of the Yugoslav People's Army which came there to defend the property of the Yugoslav People's Army, so you say they were probably using it. Do you know whether the military special unit which took over the securing of the hospital took over its use or not? Do you believe it's probable?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I said "probable," I said it in the context of what's possible, but I could personally see there were remnants of shell cases which were in the southern part of the hospital, under the windows, and you may be certain that they were not the result of work of medical experts, but rather from the people who were actively firing on the city from these very windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, how do you explain that only the glass was damaged, and that on the construction or the walls of the building, there are no such traces?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the photograph. Had we had time, we would have looked at it again. On the photograph, all you can see is damaged glass. As we heard from a previous witness, a tank shell can cause a lot of damage with a direct strike, so how do you explain that the walls were not damaged and that only the glass had shattered?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the photograph that was shown in no case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring up the photo, Exhibit P1526.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, can you see that what is mostly damaged here is glass? Where are these shells up until you came, and 200 shells after that? Where are the traces of those entry holes of tank shells shown on this building before and after you came? Can you point out one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Doctor, would you like to mark on the map -- on the photo? Please wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asked, Your Honour, to indicate what such a place could be. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you are saying that you have marked now the entry points of tank shells?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I did not state in any case that all 200 shells were tank shells. Some of them were tank shells. Most of those tank shells actually were armoured ones that would just pass through the walls and end up in other parts of the building; some in elevators, some in other areas. Most of these strikes are the results of mortar shells that hit the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But where did they enter? Did they enter from the south side? They didn't enter the front door. They had to pass through the wall. Can you show us where those 200 grenades hit the building of the Military Hospital? And you can see that the windows were broken by small-calibre weapons?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Well, that's an impression that you can have, probably. But all 200 shells did not only hit this part. There is the whole length of the southern part of the hospital. There are the surgical wards where a guided rocket entered through the window. Your Honours, I'm not an artillery expert, and I absolutely cannot speak about the consequences caused by specific artillery weapons on buildings. This is a matter for experts in that field. I, as a former JNA officer, can just assume how and in what way this destruction occurred. Perhaps I'm better acquainted with the destruction of the human body.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, sir, you saw the places from where fire was shot. You've seen the type of shells, and you've seen shells hitting the southern part of the hospital, 200 shells. And you can see here the damage on the windows. And we cannot establish what happened before the 10th of May and what happened after the 10th of May. Can we please admit this, after it is initialled and the date is placed on it? It should be a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put the date and your signature on this marked photo, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now briefly look at 1D02389. 1D2389.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that: Did you put any question in relation to the document we saw before, 1D2110?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will come back to that, but this has to do with the floors of the Military Hospital, specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just before that, we'll give the number for the marked photo.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D619.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, sir, we have a statement of yours here in "Dani" magazine. This is from the archives of "Dani." It's a Sarajevo publication, and it says here: "People have started to bypass the hospital, not only because it was on the line of sniper fire. I, as a then employee of the hospital, a Sarajevo man, was upset by the fact that patients who needed to go there didn't go there. This lasted until the moment when the Markale case occurred, when I sat in the car, went to the Clinical Centre and took the patients who were waiting up there because they couldn't wait their turn, and we were there without work. This was a crucial moment, a key moment, and then the hospital again became a city hospital, a peoples' hospital." So until Markale, you didn't actually have much to do, did you?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: We took over the hospital on the 10th of May. And during that period, we absolutely cared for the patients who were already there and patients who would come for examinations from time to time. The bulk of the patients who were wounded, according to the then transportation system, were taken to the Clinical Centre which, in a way, became the routine place where those patients were admitted. Until the Markale incident, people came in much fewer numbers to this hospital, to our hospital. But then after the Markale incident, people came in greater numbers because our hospital again became trusted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic be asked to repeat his question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking about this part of this statement and the journalist's interpretation in relation to Markale. I'm speaking about the Ferhadija case. This is a part that has to do with the Markale building, from that side of it that borders on the Ferhadija Street or the Kralja Ervasa [phoen] Street and Miskina Street. All the other Markale cases are marked as Markale cases that have to do with the market-place incident. In this context, the events in May, in 1992, when people were hit while waiting in the line, that's what that case refers to. I didn't want to correct the assumptions of the journalist, but actually the reference here was to the Ferhadija massacre and not the Markale Market incident which is close to Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, that incident is known as the incident in the Street of Vase Miskin or the incident in the bread line. There are two Markale incidents, the 5th of February, 1994, and of the 28th of August, 1995, so you need to make up your mind.

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have made up my mind. This is the one that has to do with the bread line in the Ferhadija Street, which is immediately in front of the front of the building that is referred to as Markale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not that close and it's not the way you put it, but never mind. Now, let us look at page 3 of this document, please. Can you please look at this part? I'm going to read to make it faster. As far as foreign journalist was concerned, the State Hospital was a ceaseless source of stories. The higher buildings of the central hospital building, at the same time the best position for filming, for example, of the night shelling in Sarajevo. Because of that, at one time there were four international TV companies located there, and this is how hundreds of minutes of broadcast material were filmed, pages and pages of journalists' texts were written, publications. But it was hard for anybody to be able to explain the phenomenon of Sarajevo, doctors and other medical staff?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Well, I have the privilege of referring to a friend, who was a journalist, who happened to share with me -- van Lynden, who happened to share some of the most dramatic events in my life with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes she's not sure whether she interpreted everything, because the speakers were speaking too fast and they were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since both of you are speaking the same language, put a pause between questions and answers, please. And I'm not sure -- the interpreters said they missed the last part of your question on page 52, in line 6. I think we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, how do you explain that in that situation in which you practically did not dare to stay and work in the upper floors, that there were -- in the upper floors of the Military Hospital - I am referring to it as the Military Hospital because this is how I remember it - there were four international TV companies with their crews and journalists, and this is where they filmed their footage from? So there were improvised TV studios of major international media companies. How did this happen? How was this possible in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, specifically in this case, with my permission, those crews had the possibility of staying at the top floors with prior signing of an agreement that they were doing that exposing their lives to risk and they were aware of that. If they had equipment and other things that they used in their work, in that case they would use the northern sections of the upper floors, where -- as they would only go from time to time to the southern parts of the buildings in order to film specific things. So, physically, there was no studio installed in those upper floors. These were just crews which, in a way, were broadcasting information by filming certain footage during time when this was possible. As for the rest of their time, they worked in other sections of those top floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is an unusual story here, that some boy was skipping on one foot, and he was holding his other leg in his hands, and that's how he ran into the hospital. So perhaps you can comment on this story. Can we admit this document? It's very strange for one leg to be blasted off and then to be hopping into the hospital on the other leg. That is a little bit strange. Your hospital must have seen some very strange things. It must have been the source of endless stories, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you referring to a statement which appears on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's a document, it has three pages. Perhaps the whole one can be admitted. I just indicated to two passages, and this third one, ridiculous, impossible passage, to be skipping into the hospital on one leg while the other one was spurting blood, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, the accused referred to this document as being your statement in "Dani." Can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document is an article written in the "Dani" weekly magazine about the conditions and organisation of work in our hospital. A large part of this text is the journalist's interpretation, who is retelling the text. I am insulted by the assertion that this is ridiculous that somebody could have been hopping into a hospital while carrying his other leg. This is something that I saw with my own eyes. When it says "carrying his legs," it wasn't a leg that was completely severed, but that was still partially attached by blood vessels and muscles and still partially usable. So I would not like these recollections of mine to be turned into a joke, in a way, in front of this Tribunal and to be twisted into erroneous statements before this Tribunal. That leg is reattached, that boy is still alive, he's using his leg again, and he spent the rest of the time after he recovered in Sarajevo while working as an interpreter for the international community.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Doctor, if this were true, I would not be joking, I would be horrified, and I would feel compassion. But it says here that he was carrying his other leg in his hands, in his arms. I mean, even if it was hanging by a piece of skin, you are a doctor, you know how much this must have been bleeding with a wound where the leg was severed, and it says he's rushing or dashing into the hospital, and the three operators theaters were busy, and all of that. This is not something, Doctor, that I said, but you said it. I would like to have this document admitted, and we will have more of such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You just made a statement, without putting a question to the witness, which is not acceptable, Mr. Karadzic. Do you like to respond to that assertion, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, did you state this?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: I am absolutely willing to respond to this, Your Honours, all the more so because I am a doctor myself, too, and I know how much and in what way a person can bleed, what shock is, what vaso-constriction is. But what this journalist was talking about here is his journalist's interpretation of what I said, written in a way that readers can understand it and comprehend it. The key information is that I saw the shell drop with my own eyes, and I watched this man -- young man who was holding his own limb in his own hands that was hanging off. He jumped in and was received and placed into a chair by others who helped him. So he didn't skip into the operating room. So this is not a medical interpretation of that particular case. What we are reading here is the interpretation of a particular event by a journalist in a particular kind of way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hold it, Mr. Karadzic. We'll mark this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D620.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If necessary, put your question again, but I would recommend you to move on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us move on. Can we have 1D02110, can we have it back on our screens?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, while we're waiting for that: We saw your statistics, the statistics of your hospital. In these statistics, was a distinction made between hospitalisation and mere admission and sending people back home? You had 450 beds. How many people were treated as inpatients, hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the statistics provided in my statement are based on the protocol of the Emergency Centre. It has to do with the total number of injured persons within a given period of time and their affiliation with a particular category; namely, civilians or members of the military. In other documents, there is also a reference to the actual number of persons who were kept as inpatients once they were examined. In the hospital, there are such statistics. They can always be obtained. And if that is put as a question, an answer, it can be obtained in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Doctor, that it would have been useful had that distinction been made, rather than create the impression that all of these thousands of injured persons were hospitalised? Why didn't you make that relevant statistic available if people were actually hospitalised and treated as seriously wounded?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Such statistics exist. However, the investigators did not ask for that particular information when they were speaking to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, how did you register those who were wounded in attacks launched by the BH Army or in mutual conflict?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as far as I know, we did not have any cases of treating people who were shot at at the army -- by the army. However, as for mutual conflicts, we took care of such casualties as well. They were classified according to their actual category; namely, whether they were civilians or whether they were members of the armed forces. Our classification, Your Honours, was not based on the circumstances of the wounding and the circumstances of the injury involved; that is to say, whether the injury was sustained when a person was in an apartment, in one's own apartment, in a fight, in -- on the front-line. No health institution has statistics of that kind, because in that period of time that would have been a pure loss of time, and it's not relevant for the outcome of treatment. It is the condition of the patient that is relevant as well as the assistance that should be given to the patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your medical documentation, was it kept according to forensic rules?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, as much possible in that period of time. We observed the Hippocratic Oath, and whenever possible and whenever time allowed us to do so, we practically did follow that principle of reliability and comprehensiveness of documents. When the burden was far too great, then that belonged to the second category of priorities, because life, itself, was our top priority at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we single out from your documentation those cases that were processed by applying regular forensic methodology?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: That is probably possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're going to ask the OTP to provide that for us. Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said during your interview that you did not have pathology and that post-mortems were not carried out?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: As a former military hospital, we had all the equipment for carrying out post-mortems and autopsies. However, since we did not have a qualified person for dealing with this, we just used that area as a morgue. That is where corpses were left. And from time to time, Professor Selak [phoen] or other members of his team involved in histology came from the university. Autopsies were not conducted in our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have time to ask you about Dr. Selak's fate, and you probably know about his suffering in Sarajevo. Could you please look at the circled part here. This is a State Security report. It says here: "We also know that in the evening hours on the 27th of December, 1992, there was a conflict between members of the so-called TO BiH and the HVO. The conflict occurred in the area between the tobacco factory, the School of Economics and the French Hospital, and it went on intensively for about five hours." Did you take care of the wounded and the dead from this conflict?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Before responding to this question, Your Honours, may I say that our distinguished Professor Selak is alive and well. He is a retiree in Sarajevo, and throughout the war he lived the same kind of life that I did. So it wasn't through his own free will. These were circumstances that were imposed on us. As for this highlighted area, we see that this information was provided about a conflict in a particular location between the tobacco factory, the School of Economics, and the French Hospital. I heard of this incident, but I don't see what the reason is for me to speak about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My part of the question does not include the French Hospital, but it is mentioned in your response. Doctor, when you refer to certain cases, woundings, et cetera, you assume that all of that was caused by the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours, in our protocols and in our reports, there was never any marking to that effect, that they were wounded by the Serbs. These people were categorised as wounded or injured. Who had injured them or wounded them, for ethical reasons, first of all, we don't keep such records and, secondly, we are not authorised to keep such records.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is only to be commended. But this documentation reached the Court, and that is why I have to deal with it in this way. Can the previous document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we mark it for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D621, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you have seven minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have to say on every such occasion, I will interrupt it, but I will not complete it. I will simply be stopped. This witness's statement should be rejected in its entirety, if I haven't been able to challenge it. Can the previous document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is much too fast for interpretation, and the number was not registered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It was admitted as -- marked D621, being marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, do you know a person by the name of Vesna Pagon?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know a person named Vesna Pagon. She was an employee in my hospital from May 1992 -- I don't know until which date, in particular. She is a pharmacist, and she worked in our hospital pharmacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: After the 10th of May, was she transferred to the job of a cleaner?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the 10th of May, we had been decimated. To send a pharmacist to work as a cleaner, that would mean diminishing one's own function. Vesna Pagon competently worked as a hospital pharmacist, alongside other hospital pharmacists who were then in the State Hospital of Sarajevo. She was far from being a cleaner.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw that, I withdraw that. It was a different case. Could we have 1D2112. This is an official note concerning an interview with Vesna Pagon. This other person also worked on other jobs. Well, can we have a look at this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, this is an official statement made to the police by Vesna Pagon. It says: "During the interview, Vesna told us that departures from the Muslim part of Sarajevo would be reduced to a minimum," and so on and so forth. She also said that until the beginning of 1995, a decree will be passed concerning the ban on family visits. Further on, it says Vesna referred to the example of the Sarajevo Hospital, where there are only four Serb doctors left, and their position in the Muslim part of Sarajevo is hopeless. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, what I can say to all of this is that it is a complete lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You claim that this person is not telling the truth. And she says further on that what is noticeable is that many Muslim intellectuals, as well as ordinary citizens, are being converted to Catholicism, because in that way it is easier for them to get Croatian passports. Is that a lie too?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It's an absolute lie created in the head of the mentioned lady: This has nothing to do with the actual situation. If you really want to know, in that period many people who were atheists turned to religion and to what felt safer; namely, God. It defies belief that they would convert to a different faith in order to leave Sarajevo. We stayed in Sarajevo of our own free will, and that is how we survived.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it not our practice not to admit the statements given by the third person? Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The police, given to the police. He knows the person, the witness knows the person involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness may not be the best witness to put this document through. If the accused wants to Bar Table these sorts of documents and show the relevance to each document, then we may not be opposed to that. But I don't know that this is the right witness to put the document through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is a statement given by a third person, and the current witness does not confirm anything about the document. I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll not admit this. We agree with Ms. Sutherland. Your time is up, Mr. Karadzic. How many questions do you have further?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now I'd like to put three questions. However, that will not change the position of the Defence that this witness has not been cross-examined. With all due respect to all the participants involved, way too much was invested into this witness in order for it to be possible to cross-examine him within one hour only. I would like to put three documents to him now in order to see what it is that we mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D2120, please. 1D2120.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is Vesna Pagon's next statement, and around the middle she says that: "As a positive personality, I would like to single out Abdulah Nakas, who is protecting the Serb personnel, who stayed behind, working in the hospital. He enjoys a very high reputation as a doctor, a specialist, but he does not have support because he's not a member of the SDA Party." Vesna noted that Nakas is in contact with doctors who are ethnic Serbs, his former colleagues, who are now in Serb-held territory. As for his brother, Bakir Nakas, he says that he is the opposite of Abdulah, that he turned into a major fundamentalist, which is why he often clashes with his brother. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, once again I can say that absolutely -- that this is an absolutely nebulous thing created by Ms. or Mrs. Vesna Pagon. The relations between myself and my brother were personal, and because of our professional relationship we managed to keep the hospital going throughout the war and up to the present day. Saying that I'm a fundamentalist is totally unbelievable and amazing. As far as religion is concerned, I have always declared myself as an atheist. Saying that I was a member of the SDA or that Abdulah, who is not a member of the SDA, that is not true, either, because Abdulah was a member of the SDA. Later on, he even held a high position. As a matter of fact, when there were elections for the president of the SDA when the late Alija Izetbegovic was leaving that position, he was -- he ran against the current president, Sulejman Tihic. So he was not elected president at that point in time, but as a member of the SDA he was also a Member of Parliament of our state. That was obviously his lifelong commitment. And now this prefix is being assigned to me, and I don't know why I deserve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that what she says about the late Abdulah is not true either, that this is not true, that he's on good terms with the Serbs, that he's in contact with them, and during the interview we established that he was in Pale before the 10th of May and that I had been informed that he was there, although I had not met up with him?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my brother was mobilised in the month of April, and he was sent to the then new military hospital at Sokolac. That is to say that he did not go there of his own free will, but that was the result of the will of the organs of the Yugoslav People's Army. He was and remained on good terms with the entire population of Bosnia and Herzegovina, like myself, just like Dr. Abdulah Nakas contacted colleagues from the other side, under quotation marks, I had regular contacts with Dr. Tomislav Tausan, who was the head of the Military Hospital until then, after he left, together with the other doctors in that hospital. That means that by remaining on one or the other side, our ties were not severed at all if we had to deal with normal human communications: To this day, all colleagues who went to university with me, Dr. Milan Pejic, Zdrale, all of those who were war doctors and heads of hospitals, they were my friends and we communicated on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But we have to establish one thing. Is she lying? Is she lying in your case and in the case of Abdulah, or in the case of Dr. Abdulah, she is characterising him correctly and she's characterising you erroneously?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: The part of the statement speaking about the relationship of Abdulah Nakas with Serbs is correct. The rest of that statement, the allegations are false.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that this will not be admitted either, but I personally think it could be admitted because it's a statement given to a state organ. If not, then I have to find a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Even if it is a statement given to the OTP of this Tribunal, we'll not admit this. Call your witness to confirm that content of the statement. Move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Nada Sehovac is?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps I might have heard that first and last name somewhere. But right now, I really cannot recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have her statement here. Since she's sick, she provided a notarised statement. The notary is Rama Atajic. Rama is a Muslim, isn't she? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Rama Atajic is most probably a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have her statement, in which she explains and talks about her experience in the Military Hospital, that she lived in Zadrugina, which is Omera Stupca Street now, and she tells all that happened to her after the Military Hospital was taken over. There is a statement here about the damage inflicted to the Military Hospital by the Green Berets, and the fire -- they fired at the hospital before the 10th of May. After the 10th of May, she was transferred to work as a cleaner. Before then, she was working as a lab technician, where she was in charge of washing lab equipment. Do you recall transferring her to a lower-ranking post/job?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said that I really cannot recollect the first and last name. However, according to our scale of tasks, a person who washes lab dishes can be assigned to duties as a cleaner. It's work of the same rank. And it's an unskilled position, and there is no difference between the two particular types of job. It's possible that at that particular moment, we needed more cleaners, so it was felt that somebody could be assigned to that type of job. This had nothing to do with any kind of ethnic criteria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nakas. Yes, Ms. Sutherland, did you have something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I was simply going to say what was the accused's question. And the moment I rose, he asked a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me to read one sentence from this statement: "The Green Berets surrounded the Military Hospital and opened fire at it until the Military Hospital was taken over by the B and H authorities." This means that for about a month since the official start of the war, there was daily major damage inflicted to the building by the Green Berets, and there is -- not the Serbian Army. There would be no logic to the Serbs inflicting damage to a building where there was JNA personnel and other staff who were Serbs. And then it goes on to talk about this 2nd of May interception, when they went to get the wounded by the JNA hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is simply a waste of time. You just put your question to the witness. You don't have to read out the third party's statement. Just put your question and then you can bring your witness during the Defence case. What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doctor, you said that your brothers and others informed you about what happened to the Military Hospital while you were away. Did the Green Beret surround the Military Hospital, fire at it? And you said in your statement that there was some sort of presence there in order to incite patriotism?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, definitely the hospital -- the Military Hospital was not surrounded or encircled by any forces, particularly -- well, I see that the witness stated that these were the Green Berets, and the extent and the form of that action, but I stand by my previous statement that these were local forces who were, in a way, located there, but not with any kind of objective of surrounding or in any way destroying the then Military Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. She says that upon instructions of their bosses, she cleaned the 11th and the 12th floors after the take-over, after the security of the Military Hospital left, and that she did not find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, your last question. Move on to your last document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D942. Now, I believe that the Trial Chamber will regret not allowing this witness to stay longer, because this is insufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, Doctor, this is a document. It's a bulletin by the headquarters of the Supreme Command of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 24th of October, 1993. Can we look at the third page of this document. This box text says: "Pursuant to information of the Sarajevo CSB, on the 23rd of October, 1993, at the crossroads in front of the State Hospital, a group of armed fighters of the 10th Mountain Brigade was deployed. Later checks by police patrol confirm this information. "According to unchecked information, under the command of Musan Topalovic, Caco, they intended to intercept one cistern of UNPROFOR. Allegedly, he decided on this act because the UNPROFOR were going to deliver fuel oil in return for the favour of using the water source at Pivara." Did you know that there were such brigades in the immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, this kind of information regarding the immediate vicinity of the State Hospital and other information relating to this is something that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you question the veracity of the Main Staff of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: No, I'm not doubting the credibility of that source, but I do dispute the information that you referred to here, that such information could have been accessible to me. I really do not recollect such an event, and I have no way of knowing whether this was true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you were not aware of these military targets and these events regarding the military around the Military Hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there were no events or military targets around the hospital that would jeopardise its integrity or its function. So what was happening in mutual communication and relations between the forces of the Bosnia-Herzegovina members and some members of the UNPROFOR or police is something that was not relevant, as far as I was concerned. What was of relevance to me was the function and the operation of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the next document, a statement by Tomislav Tausan, who was the previous head of the hospital. Dr. Nakas knew him personally, and he referred to him also in today's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We'll deal with this document first. This is a bulletin written by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the first page for the Trial Chamber. This is the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Supreme Command Staff of the Armed Forces, Security Administration. This is the Muslim Army or the army of that part of Bosnia that Dr. Nakas recognises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you object to the admission of this document, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Again, Your Honour, this witness is not the correct witness to be putting this document through.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With all due respect to Ms. Sutherland, we have no other better witness to speak about what is going on in front of the doors of his hospital, and this is a report by his army about events. Dr. Nakas speaks about a broad range of questions and does not know that there were military operations going on in front of his doors.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, this -- not this witness -- the Defence can put the document in another way. They can Bar Table the document, they can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I take it you do not object to the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry. If I can add, perhaps the witness has contextualised the document enough for it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. On that basis, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D622, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document 1D2116. 1D2116. This is a report on the interview of a witness, Tomislav Tausan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this Tausan the colonel who was before you at the same post?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. It would appear to be that on the basis of the name and the father's name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's look at page 3. I mean, all the pages are of interest to us, but because of speed we need to just look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at this paragraph: "There was constant sniper fire at the hospital from the Magribija Mosque, where the Muslims warehoused infantry weapons that were illegally shipped to Sarajevo. I saw when the weapons were brought in on trucks of license plates from Gorazde and then taken out of the mosque by other vehicles and distributed to Muslims. One of the more fierce attacks from this mosque on the Military Hospital occurred on the 26th of April, 1992. However, fortunately, there were no casualties. During the one of the more fierce attacks on the Military Hospital on the 3rd of May, 1992, patients were wounded," and so on and so forth. Can we look at the next page of the document, actually two pages after? Can we now look at page 5?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, you don't have to read out all these sentences. Just put your question. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to state the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: My question, Doctor, is: Was the Magribija Mosque used for military purposes, the way that Dr. Tausan described it?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, based on what I know about the Magribija Mosque is that it is a religious facility. Absolutely never was it used, nor do I have information that it was used, as a military facility or as a depot, as it is stated in this statement. As far as I know, my predecessor, Colonel Tomislav Tausan, did not leave the hospital, and all in all, I don't know from which angle and from where he could have observed trucks of such and such a license plate unloading these weapons and that these weapons were being distributed to Muslims. I don't see that. Even though I respect him as a trusted colleague, I really cannot agree with his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you agree that the Magribija Street has an exit to that part of the hospital front?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes, but you cannot see it from that part of the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. You could see Hresa from the hospital, but he could see it right in front of his nose. All right. Well, let us show you one more thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just -- just this paragraph, just this paragraph where the Unis building is mentioned. The doctor says that from the roof of the Unis building, which the doctor marked, there was firing at the Dentistry Clinic, the Gynaecology Clinic and other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this in dispute, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, when I said that there were remains of infantry weapons on the roof of the building, I was not denying that the hospital was struck by infantry weapons. I don't know though it was hit in the particular way that this witness talks about from specific positions around the hospital, because I wasn't in the hospital at the time, so this is something that I cannot confirm, this piece of information.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, one more thing. The Defence did not have time to deal with medical documents that were admitted through Dr. Nakas, but it is the position of the Defence that that documentation is not of use for legal matters because it was not kept that way. There were no investigations. It wasn't kept according to the forensic principles and techniques. There is no indication of where these people were wounded, who was wounded in conflicts, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, it is your statement. If there are some parts which you couldn't cover, it's totally as a result of your inefficient cross-examination. Ms. Sutherland, do you have some questions for your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, we have to break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please, the previous one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. It is a statement of a third person with which the witness hasn't agreed at all. We'll break for half an hour -- 25 minutes, and we'll resume at 10 to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've changed places for the computer.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Dr. Nakas, at page 50 of today's transcript, Mr. Karadzic asked you to draw on a photograph, which is Exhibit D619, the markings where the 200 projectiles hit the hospital, and you marked a number of areas where some of the shells had hit. Can I just have Exhibit P01524, the witness's amalgamated statement. And if we could -- You can see this photograph, Dr. Nakas, the one you drew on earlier today, which has -- the photograph shows the Red Cross flag. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can I take you to paragraph 22 of your statement. Or in paragraph 23, you say: "Between 1992 and 1995, the hospital was hit with over 200 projectiles." In paragraph 22, you say that the flag remained in place from May to September 1992, when the hospital removed it because of its condition. And so when Mr. Karadzic asked you to show the marks of where the 200 projectiles hit, am I correct in saying that that is not possible because of what you've stated in your statement in paragraph 22?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is correct, because that photograph is from the period from the 10th of May up until September 1992, which means that the photograph reflects what was happening in the period from May until September 1992. Everything else that happened that involved other projectiles cannot be seen on that photograph. Therefore, that photograph is a reflection of the situation in the summer of 1992, at the very outset when the hospital was taken as a target of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And that photograph depicts one part of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Absolutely, it depicts only one part of the hospital, the central part; therefore, other parts of the hospital that cannot be seen in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In that paragraph, Dr. Nakas, you said between 1992 and 1995, the hospital was hit by over 200 projectiles. And also in para 34, two pages further, you said: "The worst period of targeting on the hospital was from 13 to 16 May 1992 ...: "And: "The hospital was hit by about 40 shells of various kinds ..." So my question is how you were able to remember those numbers, 200 and 40. Did you keep a diary or did you count the number of shells?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in that period of time we were counting the shells and recording them, and we kept certain diaries of the effects. At first, we reported these occurrences to the police and to UNPROFOR. Sometimes they would come to the scene. However, later on, in spite of reports, no one came to the actual site, so, in a way, you could only record the damage sustained and try to do away with some of the consequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you think we can find those diaries made at the time?

utterances.speaker: BAKIR NAKAS
utterances.text: It is absolutely impossible to find them in a comprehensive form. These were only parts that were kept in certain daily reports and that were marked, but there is no single diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Nakas. That concludes your testimony at the Tribunal. I thank you, on behalf of the Tribunal, for coming to the Tribunal to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sutherland. Do you have something?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to note that the accused said that he'd only had one hour to cross-examine this witness. I noted that he was given two hours. And I would also ask leave to be excused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the next witness is Ms. Mulaosmanovic-Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Mulaosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Alma Mulaosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you also give us your maiden name, because this is sometimes mentioned in papers?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Alma Cehajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, you provided several statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, and you also testified before this Tribunal on two occasions. Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You testified in the trial against Dragomir Milosevic on the 6th of February, 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review this testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you affirm that the testimony accurately reflects the evidence you provided to the Tribunal in 2007?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, would you provide that same evidence to the Court if questioned on the same matters here today?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this testimony as 65 ter 90110 for admission under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be admitted as Exhibit P1551.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I would now read a brief summary of the witness evidence as admitted. Ms. Mulaosmanovic was 18 years old and a student during the events. On 27 February 1995, she was on a tram in Sarajevo that was moving from Bascarsija towards Cengic Vila. The tram was filled with civilian passengers. As the tram passed an open area, an intersection, and while the witness was facing the Marsal Tito Barracks, she heard firing from behind her, and then several shots impacted the tram. Those within the tram tried to lie on the floor to avoid being hit, but the tram was too crowded and so passengers, including the witness, could only crouch. The witness was shot and wounded in her left arm. The witness realised that the shooting came from behind her, and concluded that the shooting came from the direction of Grbavica and Vraca, areas that were controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. Ms. Mulaosmanovic was taken for treatment to a first aid station. She noticed that two elderly persons were also taken there. Ms. Mulaosmanovic felt insecure when she had to move around, but she also felt unsafe when she was at home. She would always feel to be a target and that there was no safe place in Sarajevo. She lived in a constant state of fear. Your Honour, this concludes the summary, and I would like now to address a few matters with the witness here in person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, during your previous testimony you marked quite a number of maps and photos. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to clarify one matter on one photo and one map. I would ask that Exhibit 65 ter 10199 be brought up onto the screen, please. And as it is coming up: It is a photo with some markings on it, the red markings and blue markings. Can we have that -- yes, thank you. Did you make these markings during your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What do the red markings indicate, if you start with the upper ones with the straight line?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The straight red line is the direction in which the tram was moving, the tram that I was on when this event took place, the place where the shooting started, approximately, up until the place where the tram stopped, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the red circle that you made around buildings there, what would that indicate?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: That indicates approximately the place that I thought the shooting was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these four high buildings, what are they?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: These are well-known places from where citizens were being fired at, the citizens of Sarajevo. I didn't know how to put a circle around them, because they belonged to this circle. These buildings belonged to that circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This area was controlled by which forces?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on the right side, on the very right side, we see blue markings. Can you tell us what this indicates?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Vrbanja Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit. It is a part of the 92 ter package. But as we discussed it now, I would like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted as Exhibit P1552.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would then ask that Exhibit 65 ter 10197 be brought up on the screen, please. And it is a map, as we will see, with some markings in red on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, did you make the red marks in there? And if so, what do they show?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The upper one following the yellow line also shows the direction which the tram was moving from one point to another, from the place where the gun-fire started, approximately, up until the place where the tram stopped. The circle is the place in Grbavica from where I think the firing came.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just one more question. You mentioned the Vraca [sic] Bridge when we spoke about the photo. Where would that be on this map?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I mentioned the Bridge of Vrbanja, Vrbanja Most. Can I mark it with this pen?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll use the blue colour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you much. Your Honour, I request the admission of this exhibit. This is also part of the package, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put the date of today? It's the 14th of September, 2010. Could you put the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be admitted as Exhibit P1553.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Ms. Mulaosmanovic, in your evidence, you mostly described the event on the 27th of February, 1995, and the fear you experienced. Were you living in Sarajevo throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How were the living conditions in the period from -- throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: They were very difficult, primarily for reasons of safety and security, also due to the lack of water, electricity, everything else that was needed; needed for a normal life, that is. And psychologically, a depression was felt because no one knew how long this would last. Once, a politician said sometime in 1992 that this might go on for six months, and it seemed like eternity to us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you lose any family member or friends through shelling or sniping?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: In 1992, my uncle was killed at Dobrinja. There was no electricity or gas, and that is why he was baking bread in front of the building where they lived, like other people did. A shell fell. He got killed, and his son, who was 12 at the time, I think, was wounded. Then also a girlfriend of mine was killed in the summer of 1995 on her very own balcony as she was cooking lunch. She had a fire on the balcony. Then the sister of schoolmate of mine was killed. She was perhaps 12 as well. One day, we were in school, and the teacher called out the name of Neredna Golovcanin [phoen]. And the other student said that he got killed, that he was standing at a crossroads and was hit and killed, and that he would no longer be attending school.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What effect, if any, had this fate of your relatives or friends and schoolmates have on you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very hard. It could have been any citizen, myself included. Also, my feelings for these people and for their nearest and dearest who had lost family members, these are strong emotions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this concludes the examination-in-chief, and I would now request some of the associated exhibits referred to in the tendered testimony to be admitted into evidence. In the final table that was provided to you in a filing on the 10th of September, it is clearly indicated which to be tendered and which not to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The total number of remaining associated exhibits will be three, to be clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour. Let me just double-check.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually have -- yes, that's correct, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we give them numbers right now. 10199 will be Exhibit -- why don't you give numbers. Exhibit P1554. 10200 will be Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's already admitted. So the remaining is 10198 will be -- microphone, microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 10198 will be Exhibit P1554, 10200 will be Exhibit P1555, and 09733 will be Exhibit P1556.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Karadzic, your turn to cross-examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Ms. Mulaosmanovic.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: During the war, you lived in the Street of Branka Blazek at Malta?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And which part of that street? There is Marko Marulic and there's Branka Blazek. We'll show that on the map later. Can you tell us where your apartment was?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: It was closer to Marko Marulic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And closer to the hill, right, closer to the Drinska Street? You know where Drinska Street is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that it was cloudy. What was the temperature on that day, the 27th of February, 1995? Was it cold outside?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: It was quite cold. I wore my winter jacket.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How come you were wearing Plimsolls on your feet?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: There were no precipitations that day. These were leather Plimsolls. It was dry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You entered the tram at the cathedral. How many people were there in the tram, all in all? In one statement, you said that it was quite crowded?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The tram was quite full, but in the morning when it would go into the town, it would be very, very crowded. Now, it was fairly crowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in one place that there were no soldiers in the tram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing any, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the tram driver said that right next to you, there was a uniformed soldier of the B and H Army standing next to you?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: You mean next to the driver?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, the tram driver did see a soldier in the tram when you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The driver is at the front of the tram, and I was by the third door, in the third -- in the last section of the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. So you were standing on the right-hand side of the tram? The doors are on the right-hand side; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, next to the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between you and the left wall, the left side of the tram, there were many people; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: There were people behind my back, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Behind you, next to you, and in front of you. Thus, there were people on the left side of the tram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: This was behind my back. Like I said, the tram was fairly full. It wasn't overcrowded, packed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was an investigation conducted in Sarajevo about this? Did you provide a statement? Did the police conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I was asked for -- to go to the police for an interview, where I provided a statement. I don't know about the investigation, because I left the scene immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the Bosnian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you bring that statement? Did you hand it over to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The OTP showed me that statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We would be happy if they showed it to us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How did you determine that the fires were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm surprised about this remark, because this is actually an exhibit. He received that statement. It's a statement of the 14th of April, 1995. It is given by the witness and taken by an investigator. I don't know what this remark now means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we know which investigator from the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The policeman was called Goran Kulenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask about the OTP investigator. I said which investigator it was, and was that the entire investigation? Was there any kind of investigation in Sarajevo about this?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I guess there were people in charge of that investigation. I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how did you determine that the fire came from Grbavica or from Vrace, as you said? Would you be able to decide which one was it, Grbavica or Vrace? Grbavica or Vrace?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I personally sensed that the firing was not that close, because the sound of it would have been louder. As for that, I had and I still have a scar of the entry-and-exit wound, and that is how I concluded that it came from the rear, from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the point in time when you were hit, what position were you in, your body, and especially the arm that was struck?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I was squatting, and I was holding my hands like this [indicates]. I was holding an umbrella in one hand, and I was in a kind of squatting position. It's almost like a ski position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And between the place where the tram entered -- the bullet entered the tram and yourself, was there anybody standing in between?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Most of the people dropped down, they lay down on the floor, trying to shield themselves somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us where the entry wound is and where the exit wound is on your arm?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: This is where the entry wound is [indicates], and this is where the exit wound is [indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: They're at the same height, at the same level, are they?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends how you look at it. Perhaps the exit wound is a little bit lower. That was how the hand -- the position of the hand was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said in one place that it must have been fire from the Serb territory, because had the Bosnian-Herzegovinian Army been firing, you would have heard the shots; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I think that they would have been louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The tram was moving. Does the tram produce a noise?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And so you first heard the shots, and then the bullets struck. So the initial bullets did not strike the tram, according to what you said, and then some bullets did hit the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that it was the same sound, that it was like a test burst of fire, and then the second burst of fire came which actually struck the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was a burst of fire. How many shots are there in a burst of fire, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I couldn't tell. This is a number of bullets one right after another in a sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you estimated or you were told that this was a Serbian sniper; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I don't understand weapons much. I don't know if it was a sniper or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the other participants, this is on the list of sniper incidents, F -- F15 on the list of sniper incidents, F15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What time was it when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: It was about noon. I don't know the exact time. I didn't have a watch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the speed of the tram, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I would say it was the usual, but I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's about 40 kilometres per hour?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. It's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know what -- well, perhaps it would be better for us to help you to help us to understand. Can we look at P1553, 1553 which was just admitted. Yes. We could have done without the signature, because this is going to be a Defence exhibit, but it can stay. Can we look at the basic document. This is fine, too. Ms. Mulaosmanovic, I would like to ask you to mark with a blue arrow the place of impact, and another one indicating the place where the tram stopped. Well, this is better. This new document is better. Can you indicate with a blue arrow the place of impact, and with the second arrow the place where the tram stopped? You said it stopped in front of the police station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Approximately in this part where the turning is. Actually, there are two police buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you would place an upright blue arrow in the place where the bullet impacted on you.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: I really don't know at what point in time this happened. I was crouching, you understand. I wasn't looking through the window. I can't tell you where the tram exactly was. I'm talking about this particular interval. And when that happens, time becomes relative, so each one of those intervals seems much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what is between the Serbian positions and these tram tracks, this place where this happened?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: The river is marked in blue, and that's where the line of separation was. Above the river to the north, there were different prefabricated buildings. The museums were here, there was a police station, and there were some knocked-down buildings. I don't really remember. The town has changed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you indicate these two "M" buildings? One of them is the Museum of the Revolution, and then there's the other one.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Should I mark them with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you can mark them with an arrow and a number.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is museum number 1 and then there is museum number 2.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: It's a little bit difficult to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the Museum of the Revolution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see where the Holiday Inn Hotel is?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. I don't see it. It's a little bit difficult on the map. I can see the church, but I can't really tell what the other buildings are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. And we saw where the Dobrinja Bridge is. All right, you can sign this and put the date on this document, you can initial it, and then we can switch to the photograph, because obviously this will not get us too far.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Should I put my signature on it and the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, your initials, your signature, and the date.

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted as a Defence exhibit, and then can we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D623.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at photograph number 6 from the Sarajevo-specific binder, and can we get definite 65 ter numbers, please? I will need some help with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is 65 ter 21215.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you kindly, Ms. Mulaosmanovic, to mark the buildings you recognise here, starting from the bridge on the Vrbanja, then the residential buildings, the government buildings, the faculty buildings, the museum. One of them you cannot see. Then you have the Technical School and the Holiday Inn on the other side of the tram tracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALMA MULAOSMANOVIC-CEHAJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me start from the right. With the bridge over the Vrbanja. I'm putting a "V" there [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
